title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLVIII
paragraphs:
Surely the golden hours are turning gray
And dance no more, and vainly strive to run:
I see their white locks streaming in the wind—
Each face is haggard as it looks at me,
Slow turning in the constant clasping round
Storm-driven.

Dorothea’s distress as she left church came mainly from seeing that Mr. Casaubon was determined not to speak to his cousin. Will’s appearance had only made their estrangement more obvious. She thought his coming perfectly excusable, even a kindly attempt at the reconciliation she had so often wished for. Probably he had imagined, as she had, that if they could meet naturally, they would shake hands and friendship might return. Now that hope seemed entirely lost. Will was more completely banished than ever, for being forced to see a man he refused to acknowledge must have renewed Mr. Casaubon’s bitterness.

Her husband had felt unwell that morning, with some difficulty breathing, and had therefore not preached. She was unsurprised by his near silence at lunch, and still less by his failure to mention Will Ladislaw. As for herself, she felt she could never raise the subject again. On Sundays they usually spent the hours between lunch and dinner apart. Casaubon mostly dozed in the library, while Dorothea read favorite books in her sitting room. A little pile lay on the table in the bow window, ranging from Herodotus, which she was learning to read with her husband, to her old companion Pascal and Keble’s “Christian Year.” Today she opened them one after another and could read none. Everything was dreary: the omens before Cyrus’s birth, Jewish antiquities—oh dear!—devotional sayings, the sacred music of favorite hymns. All sounded as flat as tunes tapped out on wood. Even the spring flowers and grass seemed to shiver dully beneath the afternoon clouds that intermittently hid the sun. Even her habitual sustaining thoughts carried the weariness of long future days in which they would remain her only companions. Poor Dorothea hungered for a different, fuller companionship. The endless effort of married life had increased that hunger. She was always trying to become what her husband wanted, never able to rest in his delight in what she already was. Whatever she liked, whatever she naturally wanted, always seemed excluded from her life. If her husband merely allowed it without sharing it, he might as well have forbidden it. They had disagreed about Will Ladislaw from the start. Since Casaubon’s harsh rejection of her strong feelings about Will’s claims on the family property, she had become convinced that she was right and her husband wrong, but that she could do nothing. That afternoon her helplessness numbed her more miserably than ever. She longed for people she could love and who could love her. She longed for work as directly beneficial as sunshine and rain. Instead, she seemed destined to live increasingly in a tomb, among the machinery of a ghastly labor producing something that would never see daylight. Today she had stood at the tomb’s entrance and watched Will Ladislaw retreat into the distant world of warm activity and companionship, turning his face towards her as he went.

Books were useless. Thought was useless. It was Sunday, so she could not take the carriage to see Celia, who had recently had a baby. There was no escape from spiritual emptiness and discontent. Dorothea had to endure her low spirits as she would a headache.
After dinner, when she usually began reading aloud, Mr. Casaubon suggested going to the library. He had ordered a fire and lights there, he said. He seemed revived and deep in thought.
In the library, Dorothea noticed that he had rearranged a row of notebooks on a table. He picked up a familiar volume containing an index to all the others and put it in her hand.

“You would oblige me, my dear,” he said, sitting down, “if instead of our usual reading you went through this aloud tonight, pencil in hand. Whenever I say ‘mark,’ make a cross. This is the first stage of a process of selection I have long contemplated. As we proceed, I shall explain the principles governing the choices, so that you may, I hope, take an informed part in my purpose.”

Since his memorable conversation with Lydgate, there had been many signs that Casaubon’s initial reluctance to let Dorothea work with him had given way to the opposite tendency: demanding considerable interest and labor from her. This proposal was another.

After two hours of reading and marking, he said, “We shall take the volume upstairs, and the pencil too, please. If we read during the night, we can continue. I trust this does not tire you, Dorothea?”
“I always prefer reading whatever you most want to hear,” she answered truthfully. What she dreaded was making an effort, in reading or anything else, that left him as joyless as before.

That certain qualities in Dorothea impressed themselves powerfully on others was proved by her husband’s absolute trust in her promises and in her ability to devote herself to what she thought right and best, despite all his jealousy and suspicion. Lately he had begun to regard these qualities as his own special possession. He wanted to claim them entirely.

The night reading did take place. Young and exhausted, Dorothea fell asleep quickly and deeply. Light awakened her, seeming at first like a sudden view of sunset after climbing a steep hill. Opening her eyes, she saw her husband in his warm dressing gown settling into the armchair by the fireplace, where embers still glowed. He had lit two candles, expecting her to wake but reluctant to rouse her more directly.
“Are you unwell, Edward?” she asked, getting up at once.
“Lying down made me uncomfortable. I shall sit here a while.” She added wood to the fire, wrapped herself warmly, and asked, “Would you like me to read?”
“I should be most grateful, Dorothea,” Casaubon answered. There was a little more meekness than usual in his politeness. “I cannot sleep. My mind is extraordinarily clear.”
“I’m afraid the stimulation might be too much,” she said, remembering Lydgate’s warnings.

“No, I feel no excessive excitement. Thinking comes easily.” She dared not insist. For an hour or more she read according to the evening’s plan, but moved through the pages faster. Casaubon’s mind was more alert. The slightest hint of wording seemed enough for him to anticipate what followed. “That will do—mark it,” he would say, or, “Go on to the next heading. I shall leave out the second digression on Crete.” Dorothea marveled at his mind sweeping like a bird over ground it had crawled across for years. Finally he said:

“Close the book, my dear. We shall continue tomorrow. I have delayed too long and should be glad to finish. You see, however, the principle governing my choices: to supply sufficient illustration, without disproportion, for each thesis listed in the present draft of my introduction. You understand that clearly, Dorothea?”
“Yes,” she answered, her voice a little unsteady. Her heart felt sick.
“I think I can rest now,” said Casaubon. He lay down again and asked her to extinguish the candles. Once she too was in bed, with only a dull glow from the hearth breaking the darkness, he spoke.
“Before I sleep, Dorothea, I have something to ask.”
“What is it?” she said, inwardly afraid.
“I ask you to consider carefully and tell me whether, if I die, you will carry out my wishes. Will you refrain from doing what I should disapprove of, and devote yourself to what I should want?”
The request did not surprise her. Many recent incidents had made her suspect some intention in her husband that would place another burden on her. She did not answer at once.
“You refuse?” His voice grew sharper.

“No, I haven’t refused,” Dorothea said clearly, her need for freedom asserting itself. “But it’s too solemn a matter. I don’t think it’s right to promise without knowing what the promise will require. Whatever love asked of me, I would do without a promise.”
“But you would follow your own judgment. I ask you to follow mine. You refuse.”

“No, dear, no!” she pleaded, crushed between opposing fears. “But may I have a little time to think? With all my soul, I want to comfort you. But I can’t give a pledge suddenly, especially without knowing what I’m pledging to do.”
“Then you cannot trust the nature of my wishes?”
“Give me until tomorrow,” she begged.
“Until tomorrow, then,” said Casaubon.

Soon she heard him sleeping, but sleep would not return to her. She forced herself to lie still so as not to disturb him, while a battle raged in her mind and imagination marshaled its forces first on one side, then the other. She had no suspicion that the control he wanted over her future might concern anything beyond his work. But she could see plainly that he would expect her to devote herself to sifting those mixed heaps of material, intended as doubtful illustrations of still more doubtful principles. The poor girl had completely lost faith in the reliability of the Key that had been her husband’s lifelong ambition and labor. Despite her limited education, it was unsurprising that her judgment was sounder than his. She brought unprejudiced comparison and healthy common sense to possibilities on which he had staked his whole self-esteem. Now she imagined days, months and years sorting what might be called broken mummies and fragments of a tradition itself pieced together from crushed ruins. She would sort them to feed a theory already withered at birth, like a changeling. Certainly an energetic mistake pursued energetically can keep embryonic truths alive. The search for gold also investigates substances; the body of chemistry is prepared for its soul, and Lavoisier is born. But Casaubon’s theory about the elements from which all tradition sprang was unlikely to stumble against any discoveries. It drifted among pliable guesses, no firmer than the derivations of words once thought convincing because they sounded alike, until that very likeness was shown to make the derivations impossible. His interpretive method never faced the test of creating anything that met harder resistance than an elaborate account of Gog and Magog. It could proceed as untroubled as a plan to string the stars together. And how often Dorothea had already suppressed weariness and impatience with this dubious riddle-solving, which had replaced the shared pursuit of high knowledge she thought would ennoble her life! Now she understood why her husband clung to her as perhaps his last hope of putting his work into publishable form. At first he had seemed determined to keep even her from knowing closely what he did. But gradually the terrible pressure of human need, the prospect of death coming too soon—

Here her pity turned from her own future to his past, and to his present struggle with the fate that past had created. The lonely labor, ambition barely breathing beneath self-doubt, the goal retreating as his limbs grew heavier—and now the sword visibly trembling overhead! Had she not wanted to marry him to help with his life’s work? But she had believed it would be something greater, something she could serve devotedly for its own sake. Would it be right, even to ease his grief, to labor fruitlessly on a treadmill? Could she do it, even after promising?

Yet could she deny him? Could she say, “I won’t satisfy this wasting hunger”? She would be refusing him after death what she would almost certainly do while he lived. If, as Lydgate had said was possible, he lived another fifteen years or more, her life would certainly be spent helping and obeying him.

Still, devotion to a living man differed profoundly from an undefined promise of devotion to the dead. While he lived, she would remain free to object to any demand and even refuse it. But might he intend to ask something beyond anything she had imagined, since he wanted a pledge without telling her exactly what he wished? The thought crossed her mind more than once, though she could not believe it. No: only his work held his heart. That was the purpose for which her life must extend his failing one.
And if she now said, “No! When you die, I won’t lift a finger for your work,” it seemed she would crush his already wounded heart.

For four hours she lay struggling, until she felt ill and bewildered, unable to decide, praying silently. Helpless as a child who has sought and sobbed too long, she finally slept late into the morning. When she woke, Casaubon was already up. Tantripp said he had read prayers, eaten breakfast and gone to the library.
“I’ve never seen you so pale, madam,” said Tantripp, the solidly built woman who had been with the sisters in Lausanne.
“Was I ever rosy-cheeked, Tantripp?” Dorothea asked with a faint smile.

“Well, not exactly rosy, but you had a bloom like a China rose. Always breathing in those leather books—what can anyone expect? Rest a little this morning, madam. Let me say you’re ill and can’t come into that stuffy library.”
“Oh, no, no! I must hurry,” Dorothea said. “Mr. Casaubon particularly needs me.”
By the time she went downstairs, she felt certain she would promise to fulfill his wishes. But later in the day, not yet.
As she entered the library, Casaubon turned from the table where he had been arranging books.

“I was waiting for you, my dear. I hoped to begin work immediately this morning, but I feel somewhat unwell, probably from yesterday’s excessive excitement. As the air is milder, I shall take a walk among the shrubs.”
“I’m glad of that,” said Dorothea. “I was afraid your mind was too active last night.”
“I should like it set at rest on the last matter we discussed. I hope you can give me your answer now.”
“May I join you in the garden shortly?” she asked, gaining a little breathing space.
“I shall be in the Yew-tree Walk for the next half hour,” he replied, and left her.

Exhausted, Dorothea rang for Tantripp to bring her outdoor things. She had sat still for a few minutes, but without renewing her inward struggle. She simply felt she was about to say yes to her own doom. Too weak and too afraid of inflicting a sharp wound on her husband, she could do nothing except submit completely. She remained seated while Tantripp put on her bonnet and shawl. Such passivity was unusual; she normally liked to dress herself.
“God bless you, madam!” Tantripp said. Having finished tying the bonnet, she felt an irresistible rush of love for the beautiful, gentle creature she could do no more to help.

That was too much for Dorothea’s strained feelings. She burst into tears and sobbed against Tantripp’s arm. Soon, though, she mastered herself, wiped her eyes, and went through the glass door into the shrubbery.

“I wish every book in that library was built into a cattycomb for your master,” Tantripp told Pratt, the butler, whom she found in the breakfast room. As we know, she had visited Rome and its antiquities. When speaking to the other servants she always refused to call Casaubon anything except “your master.”
Pratt laughed. He liked his master well enough, but liked Tantripp better.

Outside on the gravel paths, Dorothea paused among the nearest groups of trees, hesitating as she had once before, though for a different reason. Then she had feared her offer of companionship would be unwelcome. Now she dreaded the place where she knew she must bind herself to a companionship from which she recoiled. Neither law nor public opinion compelled her, only her husband’s nature and her own compassion: the imagined bond of marriage, not its actual requirements. She understood the whole situation clearly, yet remained bound. She could not strike the wounded soul appealing to hers. If that was weakness, Dorothea was weak. But the half hour was passing; she must delay no longer. Entering the Yew-tree Walk, she could not see him. The path curved, however, and she went on expecting to find his figure in the blue cloak and warm velvet cap he wore in the garden on chilly days. Perhaps he was resting in the summerhouse, she thought, a little way off the path. Rounding the corner, she saw him on the bench beside a stone table. His arms rested on it and his forehead lay on his arms. His blue cloak had been pulled forward, hiding his face on either side.

“He exhausted himself last night,” she thought. At first she supposed he was asleep and that the summerhouse was too damp for resting. Then she remembered how lately he had adopted this position while she read, as though finding it more comfortable than any other. Sometimes he spoke, as well as listened, with his face lowered like that. She entered the summerhouse and said, “I’ve come, Edward. I’m ready.”

He gave no sign of hearing. Thinking he must be deeply asleep, she put her hand on his shoulder and repeated, “I’m ready.” Still he did not move. With a sudden, confused fear, she bent towards him, removed his velvet cap and pressed her cheek close to his head, crying in distress:
“Wake up, dear, wake up! Listen to me. I’ve come to give my answer.” But Dorothea never gave it.

Later that day, Lydgate sat beside her bed while she talked deliriously, thinking aloud and repeating what had passed through her mind the previous night. She recognized him and used his name, but seemed convinced she ought to explain everything to him. Again and again she begged him to explain it all to her husband.
“Tell him I’ll come soon. I’m ready to promise. Only, thinking about it was so terrible that it made me ill. Not very ill. I’ll soon recover. Go and tell him.”
But the silence in her husband’s ears would never be broken again.
